basisOfRecord.quote: The functional trait approach was applied to investigate patterns of functional diversity and life-history traits of ground beetles and spiders on an alpine debris-covered glacier and along its forefield in order to describe their colonisation strategies.

Field observations and various sources, including maps, reports, aerial photographs, iconography, and records of length change collected over the last 100 years, allowed us to reconstruct the glacier tongue position during the LIA, in 1925, 1994, and 2003 (Fig. 1).
We sampled carabid beetles and spiders using pitfall traps (Eymann et al., 2010).
The traps were active over the entire snow-free seasons, from early July to late September 2011–2012.

lifeStage.quote: larval hunting strategy (surface runner, surface walker, soil pore explorer)
adult hunting strategy (zoospermophagous plant climbers, olphactory-tactil predator, visual predator)

Among carabids, the proportion of surface walker larvae gradually increased along the chronosequence of glacier retreat as described by the four classes of age of deglaciation $( R ^ { 2 } = 0 . 7 8 )$ (Table 2, Fig. 4).
Conversely, the proportion of surface runner larvae $( R ^ { 2 } = 0 . 7 3 )$ gradually decreased in relation to the time since deglaciation.
Instead, the proportion of soil explorer larvae did not change along the chronosequence.

The proportion of high dispersal species reached the highest values in the early successional stages (class 1), then gradually decreased along the chronosequence of glacier retreat $( R ^ { 2 } = 0 . 7 0 )$ (Table 2, Fig. 4).
